Early days. Honest ask.

A side project that grew — and a genuine request for feedback rather than a fanfare.

For clarity. The Government of Jersey is out to tender for an openEHR single patient record. That is a conflict too close to navigate: commvita™ is not part of that process, and will not be. And I have recused myself from being part of the evaluation panel and decision.
— Martin

Back in May I messed around with Claude and built “open community” — the start of a community-based system serving GPs and pharmacy. I’ve taken it a fair bit further in my evenings and weekends since.

It’s now called commvita™: one system covering a stable clinical community record — primary care, dentistry, ophthalmology, physio, mental health, social care — plus system flow, governance and assurance.

Why it is built the way it is. I have spent my career on both sides of this — executive and non-executive roles in digital health, as an operator buying and running these systems, and as a vendor selling them. You learn different things from each seat, and most of what I learned was about how these deals go wrong afterwards. So the design started from constraints rather than features. Seven of them, and everything else follows:

  1. It has to be open. No data lock-in. The data is yours and it must be easy to get out — openEHR as the clinical data repository and OMOP for research are the two vital constituents, not optional extras.
  2. A single product, so there is nothing to integrate. That is what delivers real-time, high-quality insight at a fraction of what a traditional estate costs. The expense was never the software; it was the joins.
  3. Configuration over customisation. One system, one codebase — sixteen jurisdictions configured from it so far, with no forks and no bespoke branches.
  4. Automation and scale, designed in. You should not be waiting weeks or months for a bug fix or a deployment.
  5. No partner tax. We integrate with third parties because the combination genuinely adds value — not because there is a toll to collect on the way through.
  6. Tools to migrate on — and off. Both directions, deliberately. A route in that has no route out is a trap, however good the product is.
  7. No long-term contracts, unless you want one. We want you to stay because you want to, and not because you can’t get out.

One system also means the whole wrap-around lives in the same place: a patient portal with research opt-in and opt-out choices that are actually enforced — not stored and ignored — a research platform with OMOP exports for study cohorts, financial recovery plans, quality impact assessments, and the golden thread from an incident on the ward to the board’s assurance framework. Pretty much whatever is needed to govern and assure a health system. This is the shape of it:

And it stopped being a solo project some time ago. I’m building this with two co-founders.

Professor Marc Farr — co-founder and Chief Data & Analytics Officer. Marc keeps pulling it towards population health and inequality; his test for every screen is whether it produces actionable insight, not another dashboard.

Hassan Chaudhury — co-founder and Chief Commercial Officer. Hassan keeps pulling it towards the commercial question: not “is it clever” but “what does it take out of the cost base”.

And behind the scenes we have a couple of shy engineering geniuses who have built it all out in Azure — ready to demo, and ready to deploy. A lot of what follows is shaped by all of them.

What you’d actually buy first

Nobody moves an EPR because the technology is better. The real barriers are migration, workflow change, clinical risk, integration, assurance, procurement, training and incumbent lock-in — and no chart is worth that. So we are not asking anyone to do it.

The first thing a customer buys is one edition, not a platform migration. Governance & Assurance stands alone for boards: incidents, risk, board assurance, policy, audit and training. Commvita Flow stands alone for operations: flow, waiting lists, discharge — what the NHS Federated Data Platform products do, on open standards, self-hosted. Either one takes feeds from the systems you already run.

The four questions a buyer actually asks.
What do I buy? One edition, starting at £1 per instance for commvita Flow, self-hosted on your own infrastructure — or commvita Governance & Assurance on a competitive basis.
What does it replace? On day one, nothing clinical. It replaces the governance or flow tooling around the record — the spreadsheets, the separate risk and board systems, the manual reporting — not the record itself.
What changes operationally? The teams already doing incidents, risk and board papers, or already running flow, do it in one place instead of several. No clinical workflow is rewritten to start.
How fast is value? Weeks, in the assurance and operational layer, because nothing has to be migrated first.

The full platform is the destination for those who choose it. The entry point is deliberately small, cheap and reversible — and if it stays a governance product for a customer forever, that is a perfectly good outcome.

Why one system — the two bikes

So why build one system at all? Because the destination matters, even when you travel to it in stages — and this is the engineering argument for the direction, not the thing we are asking you to buy on day one.

Same road, same effort. On the first bike every system is another gear, and every join between gears loses energy. On the second there is one platform and one join — the hospital EPR. If you’re an engineer, which do you design: interoperability and friction, or a single frictionless system that delivers real-time information? (It moves — give it a moment.)

I’ve always thought health systems are a bit like factories. Nobody building a factory would put a different system, by design, at the start of every production line — you’d make sure there was one. Health has ended up with the opposite: a different system at the start of every pathway, and people paid to carry information between them.

Because it is one system, the information is real time. Left shift, outcomes, flow, incident through to board assurance, quality impact assessments, financial recovery plans, training, waiting lists, safer staffing, rostering — all reading the same live record, not month-end extracts stitched together by hand.

Measured in real time, not assembled in arrears

Because it’s one system, things that normally take a programme office weeks to pull together are just… there: system flow, left shift, outcomes and digital maturity, measured as the work happens. This is the part Marc has shaped most — his standard is that population health has to end in something you can act on: a named cohort, a gap closing, an inequality measured rather than described. Captured from the running system on a seeded demonstration estate — the DEMO DATA and seeded banners in the screenshots are the platform saying so itself.

The same chain of evidence runs into the specialist corners. Genomics is the fair test, because it is the part hardest to fake: commvita holds the pedigree as data, not a drawing — sex, affection, deceased, tested and result are stored fields per family member.

Where I want challenge. The standards under the hood today are FHIR R4, SNOMED CT and ICD-10, with an ICD-11 adapter built and waiting on licensing. The openEHR side is designed and partly wired — full archetype and AQL support is the roadmap, not the present — which is exactly why I’m bringing it to the openEHR community in September and asking for a view rather than claiming the badge.

The money

This is where Hassan has pushed hardest — he saw the commercial opportunity before I’d finished describing the product, and he has kept the question honest ever since: where does the money actually go today, and how much of it does one system remove? We’ve done the modelling, and we’re confident an approach like this takes out around 80% of total cost of ownership. Not just the licences — one system is considerably cheaper than many — but the real money: the cost of feeding and watering a dozen systems, and of using people as the glue between them. The integration teams holding the seams together, the analysts re-keying between systems, the governance staff assembling packs by hand — that is the spend a single system removes.

Modelled against planning scenarios for a two-million-population system; the model and its assumptions are written down, evidence-graded, and shareable on request.

How it’s built

What this means for a customer is safe, controlled, traceable releases: every change proven against the full test suite before it ships, releases pulled by the environment rather than pushed by an engineer, and a complete audit trail from a reported issue to the deployed fix. Nobody logs into a server to release. That is table stakes for enterprise software rather than a differentiator — but on a clinical platform it is the part you would want to audit, so it is stated.

Under the hood it is deliberately boring: containers on Kubernetes, running today on Azure and Docker, with high availability on by default — replicated services, disruption budgets, spread across nodes. The pipeline runs the whole test suite plus nineteen build gates, images are built, security-scanned and published, and the cluster pulls its own updates via GitOps.

Designed for cloud portability — standard containers on Kubernetes, nothing proprietary to any one cloud. We say “designed for” deliberately: we have not yet stood up equivalent deployments on AWS or GCP, and the three clouds genuinely differ on networking, IAM, managed databases, storage and observability. We will not claim portability we have not tested.

The same pipeline runs the support loop. Every screen carries a feedback icon; a user files a bug report and it lands in a triage queue inside the platform. Every stage after that — diagnose, write the fix, test, integrate, deploy — already runs without a person touching a server. We have deliberately not closed that loop: on a clinical platform a human reviewing the change is a control, not a bottleneck. But closing it is a governance decision now, not an engineering project.

And the sixteen jurisdictions are configuration, not customisation. There are no forks and no bespoke branches: one codebase, and a versioned, source-cited jurisdiction profile that carries each country’s identifiers, terminology, regulators and statutory clocks as data. A hardcoded jurisdiction assumption fails the build. That is the difference between a product and a services business wearing a product badge: adding a country is a configuration exercise with named sign-offs, not a project.

What this would cost to build the traditional way

The codebase measures about 670,000 lines of application source (124,000 in the API, 548,000 in the web application) plus 2,200 automated test functions. Pick your own figure for what a conventional team actually finishes per developer per day once design, review, testing and rework are counted — the commonly quoted range is 10 to 50 lines. Even at the generous end that is roughly 13,000 developer-days: a team of twenty for about three years. But nobody who has watched a large health-IT programme believes the generous end — clinical safety, information governance and integration pull real delivery towards the cautious end, several times that. Put a typical blended day rate against it and the build labour alone comes to a likely minimum of £35m. Staggering — and that is before hosting, programme management, and the integration programme a many-vendor estate forces on you. This was built in evenings and weekends since May, by one person working with AI. That gap is the story.

Illustrative arithmetic, not a quotation: the line counts are measured from the repository; the productivity range (10–50 finished lines per developer-day) and the £500 blended day rate are assumptions — substitute your own and the arithmetic still sits on the page.

Jack of all trades, master of none?

A fair worry with a platform this broad. The answer is not a scoreboard — a supplier claiming to beat hundreds of competitors invites scepticism, and rightly. What we built instead is a transparency instrument: as each feature is built it is benchmarked against the named incumbents in its space, and the benchmark ships inside the software. A Competitive Intelligence catalogue anyone using the platform can open, with every rating checked against the real modules by the build pipeline so the claims cannot drift into marketing. Of 618 modules registered and 567 live, 432 are benchmarked: 256 ahead of every named competitor, 146 on par (on par somewhere, behind nowhere), and 30 behind at least one. The split matters — without it you cannot tell whether the unstated remainder is genuinely ahead or merely level. But the number worth your attention is the 30.

Where we would actually stake the claim is narrower and more useful: four workflows where the breadth earns its keep — the flow and OPEL command centre, the incident-to-board golden thread, real-time outcome and inequality measurement, and registration and access checked consistently across settings. Those are the ones to press us on.

The 30 are told straight, because a benchmark that only says nice things is marketing. Every one carries a reason in the catalogue, and they group into five kinds:

12Depth an incumbent has earned
7Not built yet
4Built, but not connected
3Our own partners
4Deliberately not competing
30behind at least one competitor

In more detail:

  1. Depth an incumbent has earned — 12. Somebody has done one thing for thirty years and does it better. An identity integration deeper and more battle-tested at hospital scale than ours; a dedicated privacy-engineering product, where we hold a policy register and no differential privacy at all; three vendors shipping a deployed length-of-stay prediction model where we ship none. That last one is instructive: an earlier version of the catalogue rated us ahead on prediction on the strength of having no model at all. That was corrected to behind.
  2. Not built yet — 7. Straightforward functional gaps, conceded. An ERP can prove a saving landed in the general ledger and commvita cannot — it records the method and the evidence a finance business partner used instead. Theatre lists, national clinical audit submissions, and the link into the national record-locator service sit here too.
  3. Built, but not connected — 4. The capability is built to the published standards and has nowhere live to talk to. Sharing records between organisations runs over national exchange networks, and joining one means being admitted as a member and issued the security credentials that let you send. We have not joined any of them yet. So the software does the honest thing and records that nothing was sent, rather than showing a success it cannot back up. Built and unconnected loses to deployed, and that is the right reading.
  4. Our own partners — 3. These are not competitors; we partner with them. Rated behind anyway, because pretending a supplier you work alongside is a rival you beat would make the whole catalogue worthless.
  5. Where we are deliberately not competing — 4. A national platform commvita feeds rather than replaces — behind by design. And two where we would rather ship nothing than ship something unverified: no pharmacogenomic content, because none has been read from source, so a deployment licenses its own; and a safe-staffing dashboard still seeded rather than wired, which cannot be ahead of a working market product.

The ratings move on measurement, and they have moved down as well as up — three fewer ahead and seven more behind since the last count. That is the assurance behind the breadth: software that stands feature-for-feature against the incumbents, and tells you in the product itself exactly where it doesn’t yet.

Assurance of commvita itself

There is a lot on this page about governance inside the platform and almost nothing about the assurance of it. If you are putting critical clinical and operational functions on someone’s software, that is the wrong way round. So here is the honest ledger.

What exists today. Clinical-safety discipline to DCB0129 with a hazard log that records its own withdrawals. Tamper-evident WORM audit chains. High availability on by default. The tested, gated release pipeline described above. The non-SaMD boundary stated in the product itself rather than in a brochure. Self-hosted deployment, so the data sits in your tenancy and your database, not on our servers.
What a buyer would rightly require, and we have not yet done. We hold no ISO 27001 certification, no Cyber Essentials certificate, no submitted DSPT, no DTAC assessment and no IHE certification. There is no independent penetration test to show you, no disaster-recovery test evidence, and no published support model with SLAs. None of that is unachievable — it is simply not done, and a first customer would be right to make it a condition.

We would rather hand you the honest work-list than a page of badges. The platform’s own registers are built the same way, which is the only reason to believe this one.

Supplier risk — and how you leave

The fair challenge to a one-platform pitch is: haven’t you just swapped many vendors for dependency on one? And behind it a harder question — what happens if this company runs out of money, or a key engineer leaves?

The answer we can evidence is that getting your data out is a product feature, not a promise. Every record is exportable over FHIR R4, including bulk $export. Research extracts come out as OMOP CDM in CSV or Parquet. These are open formats a successor system can ingest — not a proprietary dump that needs us to interpret it.

Exit thinking is in the product’s DNA rather than bolted on at the end. We ship an FDP exit-and-continuity module — tooling to help an organisation leave a different platform safely — because we think a buyer should always have a route out of anything they depend on. We would be hypocrites to build ourselves as the exception. That is a design philosophy engineered in by an operator who has lived with these systems, not by someone whose only interest is shipping you product.

Sunk cost is deliberately low: £1 per instance for the entry edition, self-hosted on your own infrastructure, with partner components behind removable seams so individual pieces can be swapped for competing products. You can integrate what you already run rather than replace it.

What we have not settled. Source-code escrow, contractual SLAs, a published support model and anything about funding or runway are commitments we have not made yet, and I am not going to imply them here. If you are a serious first customer, they are exactly the right things to negotiate — and they will be a lot more concrete in a contract than on a launch page.

You don’t have to take it all at once

To finish where this started: Governance & Assurance or Commvita Flow stand alone, and the Population Platform adds the clinical record and population health if and when you want it. Each comes with a comprehensive set of data connectors, so the systems you already run feed it from day one.

Whichever you start with, the plumbing comes with it. Digital consent and sign-off run through one e-signature service, so a quality impact assessment is approved the same way a genomic consent is granted. And a full communications CRM sits behind the clinical record, which is what makes WhatsApp, Teams, SMS and telephony one thing to operate rather than four to join up.

Third parties and integration

commvita isn’t an AI company — although it was built by AI. So we took a deliberate decision about integrations: we only integrate with parties doing something genuinely specialist — capabilities that either require separate regulation, or deep expertise of their own. And we are not going to tax that relationship. These are integrations for mutual benefit, with the health system as the primary beneficiary.

It also means the list is short on purpose. A great deal of what other suppliers sell as an add-on is simply part of the core product here — the communications CRM and its channels, e-signature and digital approvals, the patient portal, OMOP research exports, board and risk assurance. You are not buying a base licence and then buying back the things that make it usable.

That’s why we have chosen three launch partners. Spryt, for the amazing work they are doing in pathway optimisation. Rapid Health, for the groundbreaking way they are using AI to triage at a system level. And VUIT, which helps unlock the trickiest questions around health inequalities and the interventions that actually move them. We don’t expect that list to be exhaustive — but for now, it is enough to show intent.

The next milestone isn’t another hundred modules

If I am honest about where this stands: the hard part left is not building more. It is one live deployment that proves implementation, safety, adoption and the economics — and that would be worth more than everything else on this page put together. A platform with no customer is a demonstration, however much of it works.

So if you run a health system and want to be that first deployment — small, bounded, Governance & Assurance or Flow first, nothing clinical replaced on day one — that is the conversation I most want to have.

This is the three of us launching it. Marc keeps it honest on outcomes and inequality, Hassan keeps it honest on money, and I keep building in the evenings. Early days — honestly, what do you think?
